blocks.text: Why are roof trusses and bicycle frames built from triangles rather than squares? Because a triangle cannot be pushed out of shape without changing the length of a side. That rigidity is also why triangles are the foundation of all geometry.

blocks.markdown:
### The two triangle angle facts

1. The three interior angles of any triangle add up to $180°$.
2. An **exterior angle** of a triangle equals the **sum of the two opposite interior angles**.

The second follows from the first. If the exterior angle is $e$ and the adjacent interior angle is $c$, then $e + c = 180°$ from the straight line, and $a + b + c = 180°$ from the triangle, so $e = a + b$.

rows: The two base angles are equal
blocks.caption: Equal sides face equal angles — that single idea drives most isosceles questions

blocks.title: Isosceles triangles
blocks.text: If the vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is $40°$, the remaining $180° - 40° = 140°$ is shared equally between the two base angles, giving $70°$ each. Always subtract the odd angle first, then halve.

blocks.caption: Pythagoras' theorem: c is the hypotenuse, the side opposite the right angle

blocks.title: Using Pythagoras' theorem
blocks.prompt: A ladder 10 m long leans against a vertical wall with its foot 6 m from the wall. How far up the wall does it reach?

steps.text: The wall, the ground and the ladder form a right-angled triangle. The ladder is the hypotenuse, because it is opposite the right angle.
Write Pythagoras with the unknown height h.
Take the positive square root, since a length cannot be negative.

blocks.title: Add or subtract?
blocks.text: **Add** the squares only when you are looking for the hypotenuse. When a shorter side is unknown, you must **subtract**. Identify the hypotenuse first — it is always the side opposite the right angle, and always the longest.

blocks.markdown:
### Polygons

A polygon with $n$ sides can be cut into $n - 2$ triangles from one vertex, so

$$\text{sum of interior angles} = (n - 2) \times 180°$$

For **any** polygon, the exterior angles always add to $360°$. So for a **regular** polygon with $n$ sides:

$$\text{each exterior angle} = \frac{360°}{n}, \qquad \text{each interior angle} = 180° - \frac{360°}{n}$$

blocks.title: Go through the exterior angle
blocks.text: To find the number of sides from a given **interior** angle, first convert to the exterior angle by subtracting from $180°$, then divide $360°$ by it. An interior angle of $150°$ gives an exterior angle of $30°$, so $n = 360 \div 30 = 12$ sides.

points: The interior angles of a triangle add to 180°.
An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
In an isosceles triangle the two angles opposite the equal sides are equal.
Pythagoras' theorem, $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, applies only to right-angled triangles.
Add the squares to find the hypotenuse; subtract to find a shorter side.
Interior angles of an n-sided polygon sum to $(n-2) \times 180°$, and exterior angles always sum to 360°.
